newsitem.title: USA: Stainless steel mills set to feel the pinch.
newsitem.headline: Stainless steel mills set to feel the pinch.

text.p: Rising stainless steel production will tip the global market into a significant surplus by the year 2005, putting strong downward pressure on prices and profitability for mills, Firoze Katrak of Charles River Associates said.

"We are in a world where profit margins and prices will deteriorate," Katrak told delegates in a presentation on the long term steel outlook at Ryan's Notes vanadium, molybdenum and columbium conference, three ferro-alloys used in steelmaking.
Total global consumption of stainless steel is about 12 million tonnes a year of finished product, following historic growth of 5 percent a year.
"Growth in consumption of stainless steel will slow down to less than 2 percent a year sometime early in the next century," Katrak said.
There was also a trend away from the nickel containing austenitic stainless steels to the ferritic types, especially in construction, he added.
Consumption growth in Western Europe, Japan and Korea will slow down as it grows in Asia and China.
Production was set to rise in all regions of the world, except in Russia. The oversupply of flat products was most acute in Western Europe.

There will be very little difference in cost competitiveness between the world's stainless mills in coming years, and the only significant cost advantages will be reaped by those who move to direct casting of stainless strip.
"Direct strip casting will be a serious threat to many existing producers early in the next century," Katrak said.
Nucor (RIC) is set to start up its direct strip stainless facility soon, and such projects will herald a "severe decline in prices down the road within five years," Katrak added.

Suppliers of ferro-alloys and stainless steel scrap will also bear some of the brunt from weaker steel prices as mills try to buy cheaper raw materials, and suppliers of the latter may face more bankruptcies, Katrak warned.
More stainless steel scrap will also be used at the expense of primary ferro-alloys, Katrak said.
